claim: Wild New Caledonian crows make hook tools to a standard pattern (hooked twigs, stepped pandanus tools) with population-level handedness, and designs differ between populations (5550 tools, 21 sites, 3 designs).
agent_test: Seed a library with a few named standard tool templates; compare success and tokens against free-form generation per task at equal tokens.

claim: The 2002 Betty wire-bending event is a single accidental observation (N=1); wild crows routinely bend stems (10 of 18 temporarily captive wild crows bent a new hook shaft), so 'novel invention' is contested and shaping is not excluded.
agent_test: Do not treat one-off tool invention as evidence; require first-use success over many tasks.

claim: Replication of bending/unbending in 17 captive crows found only a minority solve (3 of 10 made hooks, 1 straightened consistently; 4 of 10 solved the Z-tool at least once, 2 consistently), with differing mechanisms.
agent_test: Report per-task solve rate over many seeds, not best-of runs.

claim: Four hand-raised rooks, a species that does not use tools in the wild, all bent wire into a hook (3 of 4 on trial 1), so hook making does not need a tool-using ecology; but only 35% of attempts retrieved the bucket and bend angle mattered (100 vs 75 degrees).
agent_test: Check the agent verifies a made tool against a functional criterion (tests) before using it.

claim: Naive juvenile crows reared without adults develop tool manufacture with inherited action patterns; social demonstration changes object handling and preferences but is not required.
agent_test: Not testable on an LLM directly; informs why a built-in prompt to try tool-making should be explicit in the schema.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-03 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Crows pass first-trial tests of tool reasoning: metatool use (4 of 7 on trial 1), compound tool construction (4 of 8 naive birds, transfer to new materials), and out-of-sight multi-stage metatool problems (criterion 16/20). Compound-tool need test re-verified from the paper text: uncombined tool tried first on 70.8% (food close) vs 20.8% (food distant), per-bird Fisher p 0.037, 0.001, 0.100, 0.193 (d18).
agent_test: Give the agent a task needing a tool built from parts never shown in use; score first-attempt success.

claim: Planning with tools in crows is not one-shot: stone metatool criterion needed 43 to 69 trials and the stone condition was much harder than the stick condition.
agent_test: Measure attempts to criterion, not only final accuracy.

claim: Crow insight claims fail feedback-removal tests: horizontal string pulling was not solved (8/11 chose the connected string on trial 1, p=0.11; only one crow completed experiment 1; humans 49/50), supporting a perceptual-motor feedback account.
agent_test: Remove intermediate feedback from a task and test whether tool use survives; this separates planning from reactive chaining.

claim: Aesop's fable results are explained by an initial functional preference plus learning from successes: pooled 5 articles (32+ experiments) show learning from success but not failure and no transfer; magpies reached significance only in late trials.
agent_test: Use this null model as the baseline for any claim that the agent reasons about tools.

claim: Maker-user split works on procedural tasks: GPT-4 makes a Python tool once and GPT-3.5 Turbo then matches GPT-4 (CoT to LATM: Logical 66.4 to 79.7, Tracking 61.6 to 99.6, Dyck 20.4 to 92.2, Word Sorting 59.2 to 98.3, CRT 0 to 100, Schedule 18.9 to 100). For GPT-4 as user LATM is flat on Logical (88.8 vs 86.6).
agent_test: Make a tool once with a strong pass on training items, reuse on held-out items cheaply; compare at equal total tokens including making cost.

claim: Tool making fails for weak makers and weak users: GPT-3.5 as maker failed all 5 trials on Logical Deduction and Tracking (tool fit only training samples); verification repaired only 2 of 60 trials; weaker users (davinci to ada) fall to near zero on hard tasks.
agent_test: Test each new tool on fresh items before storing; reject tools that only fit the training samples.

claim: Separating tool creation from use with a rectification step helps: ChatGPT TabMWP 91.6/93.5 (entangled, no-CoT/CoT) vs 90.5/94.7 (CREATOR); rectification lifts program-of-thought 80.0 to 87.3; transferring a correct tool across scenarios raised accuracy 63.0 to 78.3. Gain from separation itself is small.
agent_test: Ablate rectification (error-driven repair) at equal tokens.

claim: A task-specific library of verified, abstracted, deduplicated snippets retrieved by several views helps (CRAFT average 43.16% relative F1 gain), but generic libraries (NumPy, SymPy) did not help, and BM25 retrieval matched CRAFT on homogeneous TabMWP (89.2 vs 88.4).
agent_test: Compare task-relevant library, generic library and no library at equal context budget.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-03 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: A growing verified skill library with self-verification and curriculum drives open-ended progress in Minecraft (63 items in 160 iterations, 3.3x; wooden/stone/iron 15.3x/8.5x/6.4x; random curriculum -93%, no self-verification -73%). The library alone is not enough.
agent_test: Ablate verification and library separately in a multi-task run.

claim: Skill caching saves tokens on compositional tool tasks even when skill making is charged (126 tasks, GPT-5.2 1.23M to 0.26M tokens, -79%, success 87% to 90%; Claude 4.5 Sonnet -71%; Gemini 3 Pro -54%; one model only -11%). Hierarchical skills are model dependent: GPT-5.2 success is 90% flat but 79% nested, equal for Claude 4.5 Sonnet, better for DeepSeek-V3.2 (87 to 92 of 126); nested costs more tokens in all three.
agent_test: Test flat versus nested skill reuse on at least two benchmarks and three models; measure error propagation and tokens including making cost.

claim: Tool documentation beats demonstrations: with docs, zero-shot equals 12 to 16 shot on TabMWP and NLVRv2; demos cause copying of familiar flags (-P instead of --port).
agent_test: Store tools with a short doc versus worked examples at equal tokens.

claim: Learned tool USE is not tool making: Toolformer (6.7B) called tools in about 98% of eligible cases and beat GPT-3 175B on LAMA and math, but only above about 775M parameters and with one call per input.
agent_test: Excluded by the no-training constraint.

claim: LLMs are weak at innovating tools: children 3-7 pick the non-obvious tool 85.2% and adults 95.7% while LLMs pick the similar-looking distractor; GPT-4 on MacGyver gives efficient solutions 18.9% and infeasible 37.5%, wrong tool usage is 42.4% of errors.
agent_test: Run a MacGyver-style subset and measure the effect of an explicit step that checks each object's function against constraints.

claim: Step-wise reflection and divergent-convergent prompting help on MacGyver: GPT-4 infeasible answers fall 9.7 points with reflection; div-conv raises efficient answers 6.5 points; reflection helps only the strongest model. Boundary: reflection did not reduce infeasible answers for the two weaker models tested (Claude2, Llama2-13b); divergent-convergent helped all (d17). No current-model test found.
agent_test: Add a per-action feasibility check at equal tokens.

claim: Recognition of a buildable tool falls with model size: Qwen3.5 recognition 0.29, 0.10, 0.05, 0.02 (2B to 27B) while win rate rises 0.46 to 0.88; larger models solve by hand and stop calling tools (no-call episodes 61 to 154 of 180). Model-family dependent and a July 2026 preprint. A prompt stating that exactly one listed tool solves the task restores recognition (Qwen3.5 27B 0.02 to 0.60, Qwen2.5 32B 0.15 to 0.89, Qwen3 32B 0.06 to 0.85), so the effect is mostly not looking, not not seeing (d15). Opus builds less than Haiku, but no extended-thinking test exists (d16).
agent_test: Add a forced 'is a tool listed or buildable for this' step before solving by hand; run at equal tokens on current reasoning models with extended thinking on and off.

claim: Automatic tool building with closed-loop self-repair is feasible (ToolMaker 12/15 vs 3/15 for OpenHands, 0.94 USD per tool), and simulated trial and error with long-term memory lifts a 7B model to 76.8% on ToolBench APIs above GPT-4 ICL 60.8%.
agent_test: Test a self-repair loop with unit tests as stopping rule at equal tokens.

claim: TroVE (full text re-read): the '79-98% smaller toolboxes' is versus other methods (e.g. 16 to 38 tools vs CRAFT 181 to 525, CREATOR 875 to 4,595). Periodic trimming cuts its own library 74-90% with a small accuracy loss. A no-reuse INSTANCE baseline (395 functions on GQA) fell 0.21 below primitives-only. Open 7B model and GPT-4; CRAFT scored 0.45 vs TroVE 0.44 on GQA.
agent_test: Add periodic pruning of unused tools; measure accuracy and context size.

claim: Tool use is a spectrum between flexible and stereotyped, and an intrinsic urge to combine objects may precede tool use; hooked-stick tools appear limited to specific crow populations (review, no new numbers).
agent_test: Narrative only; no direct test.

claim: Models decide to build a tool too early. With four current models (Haiku 4.5, Opus 4.8, GPT-5.4-mini, GPT-5.6 Sol) the share of first-sight commits was 28/4/15/24% in an abstract game but 100/99/88/100% when the commit meant writing a reusable script; a PPO-trained 14B model lost the skill on numeric problems.
agent_test: Add a 'has this task type recurred or will it?' gate before any tool is made; measure first-sight builds with and without the gate at equal tokens.

claim: Library size has no single answer: with no reuse control, hundreds of functions hurt (TroVE INSTANCE, 395 functions on GQA, -0.21 vs primitives); with multi-view retrieval, accuracy rose through 261, 337 and 525 tools (CRAFT). Retrieval plus de-duplication plus trimming, not size, appears to decide the sign. No sweep above 525 on a modern model with a fixed budget exists.
agent_test: Sweep library size 0 to 1,000 behind top-k retrieval versus full-context listing on a current model with a fixed token cap.

claim: Verification before storage is not isolated by any study found. Voyager's self-verification ablation (-73% items) also controls when to move on; ReGAL ablates later edit and prune steps (Date 77.0 to 69.6 without edit, 65.5 without prune; TextCraft 34.1 to 25.3 without prune) but not the verify gate; AllocBench relays a claim that library methods mostly gain from self-correction.
agent_test: Fix a library; toggle test-on-fresh-items before storage and toggle retrieval; compare at equal tokens.

claim: A post-storage edit-and-prune cycle helps: ReGAL ablations show losses of 3 to 12 points when pruning is removed, and under a distribution shift pruning alone gave +3.5 points on TextCraft with a further +2.3 from re-learning (open CodeLlama-13B, small test set).
agent_test: Add a periodic review that prunes tools with a low pass rate; measure on a shifted task mix.

claim: Specifying the tool interface helps the maker: CREATOR with utility plus input/output hints reached 75.7 vs 63.8 without (ChatGPT, Creation Challenge), and CRAFT shows abstraction and good function names matter (abstraction removed costs about 8 points on GQA; removing names costs over 6.6). No study compares fixed tool templates with free-form making.
agent_test: Compare a fixed template (name, purpose, inputs, outputs, test) against free-form making at equal tokens.

claim: No LLM study was found that runs crow-style tasks (compound tool construction, out-of-sight metatool stages, Aesop's fable) with the Hennefield and Ghirlanda null model, nor a current reasoning-model test of MacGyver reflection or a template-versus-free-form tool-making comparison (limited search; arXiv and citation APIs were rate-limited).
agent_test: Build the crow-style tasks as a small harness: first-trial success versus learned success over repeated trials.
